claims.text: The baseline is a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate.
The baseline coating has a uniform microstructure.
Overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding are governed by dislocation glide and grain-boundary sliding.
Nanoscale precipitates influence dislocation glide and grain-boundary sliding.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates enhances the proposed atomic-scale deformation mechanism.
The controlled modification is the introduction of 2 vol% uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates.
The introduced precipitates have a size of 10 nm.
The introduced precipitates may be Cr-rich.
Dislocation density and grain-boundary structure mediate the effect of precipitates on sliding behavior.
At 600°C, 1 m/s sliding speed, and 10 N normal load, the precipitate-containing coating will have 25% greater wear resistance than the precipitate-free baseline.
At 600°C, 1 m/s sliding speed, and 10 N normal load, the precipitate-containing coating will exhibit 30% less microscopic deformation than the precipitate-free baseline.
The predicted effects should hold over temperatures from 500°C to 700°C.
The predicted effects should hold for sliding distances up to 1000 m.
Coating thickness, substrate material, and testing environment may alter the proposed deformation mechanisms and resulting outcomes.
The hypothesis is falsified if wear rate is reduced by less than 15% and microscopic deformation is reduced by less than 20% relative to the precipitate-free baseline.

contradictions.description: The precipitates are said to enhance dislocation glide and grain-boundary sliding, while also reducing microscopic deformation. No explanation distinguishes beneficial control or obstruction of these mechanisms from an increase in their activity, so the stated mechanism and outcome are in tension.

The predictions specify 25% greater wear resistance and 30% less deformation, but the falsification thresholds are only 15% lower wear rate and 20% less deformation. Results can therefore substantially miss the quantitative predictions without falsifying the hypothesis. The conjunctive wording also requires both thresholds to fail, so failure of either individual prediction alone is not decisive.
